title: Chapter XXXVII

teacherSummary.text: Darcy and Fitzwilliam leave Rosings. Lady Catherine notes Elizabeth's low spirits. Elizabeth rereads Darcy's letter, ashamed of her family's conduct and sympathetic now to Darcy's objections.

vocabulary.context: How grievous then was the thought that, of a situation so desirable in every respect, so replete with advantage, so promising for happiness, Jane had been deprived, by the folly and indecorum of her own family!
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “indecorum”: in- (Latin in-, "not" or "in"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: “Oh!—Your uncle!—He keeps a manservant, does he?—I am very glad you have somebody who thinks of those things.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “manservant”: man (Latin manus, "hand") + -ant (Latin -ans, "one who, doing"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: The quality or state of being giddy
vocabulary.context: Her father, contented with laughing at them, would never exert himself to restrain the wild giddiness of his youngest daughters; and her mother, with manners so far from right herself, was entirely insensible of the evil.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “giddiness”: -ness (Old English -ness, "state of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: Face to face, or front to front
vocabulary.context: Catherine, weak-spirited, irritable, and completely under Lydia’s guidance, had been always affronted by their advice; and Lydia, self-willed and careless, would scarcely give them a hearing.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “affronte”: af- (Latin ad, "to"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To bring back to its former state
vocabulary.context: Darcy’s explanation, by restoring Bingley to all her former good opinion, heightened the sense of what Jane had lost.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “restore”: re- (Latin re-, "back, again"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: Anxiety on Jane’s behalf, was another prevailing concern, and Mr.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “prevailing”: pre- (Latin prae, "before") + -ing (Old English -ing, action). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: When they parted, Lady Catherine, with great condescension, wished them a good journey, and invited them to come to Hunsford again next year; and Miss de Bourgh exerted herself so far as to curtsey and hold out her hand to both.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “exert”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: Acting contrary to the standard of right
vocabulary.context: When she remembered the style of his address, she was still full of indignation; but when she considered how unjustly she had condemned and upbraided him, her anger was turned against herself; and his disappointed feelings became the object of compassion.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “unjust”: un- (Old English un-, "not"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: Catherine, weak-spirited, irritable, and completely under Lydia’s guidance, had been always affronted by their advice; and Lydia, self-willed and careless, would scarcely give them a hearing.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “irritable”: ir- (Latin in-, "not") + -able (Latin -abilis, "able to be"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To become greater or more in size, quantity, number, degree, value, intensity, power, authority, reputation, wealth
vocabulary.context: His attachment to Rosings certainly increases.”
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “increase”: in- (Latin in-, "not" or "in"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

context.history: Travel by coach gave time for reflection and social mixing.

significance: Elizabeth's quiet reflection marks her inner change.
discussionQuestions: How does Elizabeth seem different now?
Where does characterization appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with pride and self-knowledge?

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter XXXVII,” how does Austen show leaving Kent? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: High School / Common Core
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter XXXVII develops the idea of leaving Kent. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of characterization and tone / mood shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Jane Austen uses characterization in Chapter XXXVII to complicate the reader's understanding of leaving Kent. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter XXXVII within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of leaving Kent responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter XXXVII as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of leaving Kent. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Pride and Prejudice.

satQuestions.passage: Their first subject was the diminution of the Rosings party. “I assure you, I feel it exceedingly,” said Lady Catherine; “I believe nobody feels the loss of friends so much as I do. But I am particularly attached to these young men; and know them to be so much attached to me!—They were excessively sorry to go! But so they always are. The dear colonel rallied his spirits tolerably till just at last; but Darcy seemed to feel it most acutely, more I think than last year. His attachment to Rosings certainly increases.”
satQuestions.prompt: Which choice best states a central concern of “Chapter XXXVII”?

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: How does Elizabeth seem different now? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are indecorum, manservant, giddiness, affronted, restoring. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check Webster's. Here is the first: “How grievous then was the thought that, of a situation so desirable in every respect, so replete with advantage, so promising for happiness, Jane had been deprived, by the folly and indecorum of her own family!” Webster's says: Want of decorum. Now the word history: “indecorum”: in- (Latin in-, "not" or "in"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “manservant”: man (Latin manus, "hand") + -ant (Latin -ans, "one who, doing"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary. “giddiness”: -ness (Old English -ness, "state of"). Root not in our table: have students find it. Add each root to your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Pride and Prejudice would have known. Travel by coach gave time for reflection and social mixing. Why does this chapter matter? Elizabeth's quiet reflection marks her inner change. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for characterization.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. I read a sentence, stop, and ask what the author is doing. When I see characterization, I underline it and write in the margin what effect it has. Here I notice the diction and the sentence rhythm, and I connect them to leaving Kent.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Characterization, Tone / mood, Plot.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of characterization. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.
segments.passage: Their first subject was the diminution of the Rosings party. “I assure you, I feel it exceedingly,” said Lady Catherine; “I believe nobody feels the loss of friends so much as I do. But I am particularly attached to these young men; and know them to be so much attached to me!—They were excessively sorry to go! But so they always are. The dear colonel rallied his spirits tolerably till just at last; but Darcy seemed to feel it most acutely, more I think than last year. His attachment to Rosings certainly increases.”

segments.script: Your turn. Annotate the next page in the app for Characterization, Tone / mood, Plot: at least three marks with a margin note each. Then open your writing prompt; your level is already set. Middle-school version: In “Chapter XXXVII,” how does Austen show leaving Kent? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence. I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion (think-pair-share or a short Socratic circle).
segments.script: Let's talk. Our question: How does this chapter connect to first impressions and prejudice? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the chapter quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about leaving Kent, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how characterization shapes leaving Kent. Tonight, read the next chapter and add two words to your etymology log.
